lines.text: In 1731, Philadelphia had no lending library.
No fire company. No hospital. No college.
Twenty years later, it had all four, and one man had helped to start every one of them.

lines.text: Benjamin Franklin: printer, writer, scientist, inventor.
And in time, a Founding Father, who signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
A polymath, pointed at the public good.
It began with the Junto: a club of young tradesmen he gathered in 1727, to read, debate, and improve themselves.
First, they pooled their own books. Then, in 1731, Franklin persuaded fifty subscribers to pay forty shillings each, and buy books together.
The Library Company of Philadelphia is still open today: America's oldest cultural institution.
Fire was the next problem.

lines.text: After warning that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, he organised the Union Fire Company: volunteers pledged to fight fires with their own leather buckets.
When Dr Thomas Bond wanted a hospital for the sick poor, Franklin found a clever way to fund it.

lines.text: The Assembly would give two thousand pounds, but only if private donors raised two thousand first.
It was one of America's first matching grants.
Then came an academy, which grew into the University of Pennsylvania.

lines.text: Each one had to be built from scratch: the agreements, the subscriptions, the fundraising, the books.
Franklin did it four times, alongside a printing business, an almanac, and experiments with lightning.
Today, a founder like Franklin would not have to start from zero.

lines.text: A fiscal sponsor gives a new project a legal and financial home from day one: it can accept gifts, win grants and sign contracts, while the founder does the work.
That is what Mulvium is building: a home for the next Franklin.
